Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 2:

﴿Those who are humble and submissive in their prayer.﴾ Khushu' (humble submission) is a state in the heart of fear, watchfulness, and lowliness before the greatness of the Lord, may His majesty be exalted. Its effect then appears upon the limbs in stillness, devotion to the prayer, not turning the head (aside), weeping, and supplication. Some jurists have counted khushu' among the obligatory elements of the prayer, because they took it to mean the presence of the heart in it. A hadith says: "A servant is only recorded for what he understands of his prayer." The correct view is that khushu' is something additional to the presence of the heart, for the heart may be present and yet not be humble.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 23, verse 3:

﴿Who turn away from vain talk﴾. Al-laghw (vain talk) here means: worthless speech, such as abuse and idle amusement, and speech about what does not concern one. The number of kinds of speech that are forbidden is twenty. The meaning of turning away from it (al-i'rad) is: not listening to it and not engaging in it. It is possible that he means they do not speak it themselves, but their turning away from listening to it necessarily implies that, and all the more so.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 4:

﴿لِلزَّكَاةِ فَاعِلُونَ﴾ meaning: paying (zakah). [Ibn Juzayy's] "meaning: those who pay." If it is said: why did He say "fa'ilun" (doing) and not "mu'addun" (paying)? The answer: zakah has two meanings. One is the act that the one who pays zakah performs, namely the payment of what is due on wealth. The other is the amount extracted from the wealth, as in your saying: "This is the zakah of my wealth." The intended meaning here is the act, due to His saying ﴿فَاعِلُونَ﴾. The other meaning is also valid with an omitted element, whose sense is: they are doers of the payment of zakah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verses 5–11:

﴿عَلَىٰ أَزْوَاجِهِمْ﴾ This prepositional phrase (majrur) is connected to a verb implied by his saying ﴿غَيْرُ مَلُومِينَ﴾, meaning: they will not be blamed regarding their wives. It is also possible that it is connected to ﴿حَافِظُونَ﴾, with ʿalā (على) taking the meaning of ʿan (عن), meaning: they guard [themselves] from [anything other than] their wives.

﴿أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ﴾ means: the women who are owned (al-mamlukat, the enslaved women).

﴿وَرَآءَ ذٰلِكَ﴾ means: other than the wives and the enslaved women.

﴿لأَمَانَاتِهِمْ وَعَهْدِهِمْ﴾ may mean their trusts (amanat) and their covenants (ʿahd) with people, and the trust and covenant of Allah in His religion; or it may be general. The amanah (trust) is more general than the ʿahd (covenant), since a trust may be held by a covenant or without a prior covenant.

﴿رَاعُونَ﴾ means: they keep them, and they are steadfast in upholding them.

﴿عَلَىٰ صَلَوَاتِهِمْ يُحَافِظُونَ﴾: to be steadfast over the prayers (al-muhafazah) is to perform them at their proper times while fulfilling their conditions (shurut). If it is asked: how is the mention of the prayers repeated, at the beginning and at the end? The answer is: it is not a repetition, because the first mention concerned humility (khushuʿ) in them, and the mention here concerns guarding them; the two are different. In both places the prayer is attributed to them, indicating the firm establishment of their performing it.

﴿ٱلْوَارِثُونَ﴾ means: those who deserve Paradise. The inheritance (al-mirath) is a metaphor. It has also been said that Allah has made for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in Hell, so the believers inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers in Paradise.

﴿ٱلْفِرْدَوْسَ﴾ is the city (madinah) of Paradise, and it is the Garden of grapevines (jannat al-aʿnab). He returned the pronoun to it in the feminine, according to the meaning of "Paradise" (al-jannah).

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verses 12–14:

﴿And We certainly created man﴾. It is disputed whether this refers to Adam or to the human species (jins Bani Adam). ﴿from an extract of clay﴾. The sulalah (extract) is what is drawn out of a thing, that is, what is extracted from it, which is why it is said to be the essence. What is meant here is the portion taken from the clay from which Adam was created. If by "man" Adam is meant, then the meaning is that he was created from that extract taken from the clay. But His later words ﴿then We made him a nutfah (drop)﴾ must refer to the children of Adam, so the pronoun returns to something other than what was mentioned first, though the context of the speech makes this clear. If by "man" the son of Adam is meant, then the return of the pronoun to him is sound, and the meaning of creating him from an extract of clay is that his origin was created, and his origin is his father Adam. In my view it is also possible that "man" refers to the species that encompasses Adam and his offspring. He first mentioned man in general, then detailed it afterward into the creation specific to Adam, which is from clay, and the creation specific to his descendants, which is the nutfah. If it is asked: what is the difference between the first min (من) and the second min (من)? The answer, as al-Zamakhshari stated, is that the first min indicates the starting point (ibtida'), and the second indicates explanation (bayan), like the phrase "from the idols" (min al-awthan).

﴿in a firm lodging﴾, meaning the womb of the mother. The meaning of ﴿makin (firm)﴾ is "settled," and this is in reality an attribute of the settled nutfah, not an attribute of the place in which it settles, but it is like your saying "a traveled road," meaning people travel along it. The explanation of the nutfah, the mudghah (lump of flesh), and the 'alaqah (clinging clot) has already been given at the beginning of al-Hajj (surah 22).

﴿another creation﴾. It is said that this is the breathing of the soul into it. It is also said that it is its coming out into the world. It is also said that it is the attainment of youth. And it is said in general terms that it is from the breathing of the soul into it until its death.

﴿So blessed is Allah﴾. The word is derived from barakah (blessing). It is also said that its meaning is "sanctified" (taqaddasa).

﴿the best of creators﴾, meaning the best of creators in creation. The specification (tamyiz) has been omitted because the speech indicates it. Some interpreters explained "the creators" as "those who determine," to avoid describing the created being as a creator. However, it is not necessary to deny that the created being is a creator in the sense of a maker, as in His words ﴿and when you shape from clay﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 110). What must be denied of the created being is the meaning of invention and bringing into existence from nothing, and this is the very thing in which Allah alone is unique.

﴿عَمَّا قَلِيلٍ﴾ "In a little while" — the word *ma* here is superfluous (*ma za'ida*, an extra particle that adds emphasis without changing the meaning). It is also said that it is a qualifier of time, and the sense is: "after a little time, they will become regretful."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 41:

﴿So We made them a debris of rubbish (ghuthaʾ)﴾, meaning: destroyed, like the ghuthaʾ. The ghuthaʾ is what the torrent carries of leaves and other things that decay and turn black, so the destroyed are likened to it. ﴿So away with them!﴾ — bu'dan is a verbal noun (maṣdar) occupying the place of the verb, meaning "they were removed far away", i.e. they perished; and its governing verb is an implied one that does not appear.

﴿تَتْرَا﴾ is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of the pattern *fa'lā*, and its meaning is successiveness and consecutiveness. It occupies the position of a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), meaning: coming in succession, one after another. Whoever reads it with *tanwīn* (nunation), its *alif* is for affixation (*ilḥāq*). Whoever reads it without *tanwīn*, its *alif* is for the feminine, so it is not inflected (*lam yanṣarif*). Its feminine form is because the messengers are a group, and the first *tā'* in it is a substitute for a *wāw*, which is the first radical of the word (*fā' al-kalima*).

﴿وَجَعَلْنَاهُمْ أَحَادِيثَ﴾ means that people speak of what befell them. It may be the plural of *ḥadīth* or the plural of *uḥdūthah*, and the latter is more fitting, because it is said of evil.

"Proud, arrogant people" (qawman ʿalin): i.e., haughty tyrants. "And their people are servants of Us" (wa-qawmuhuma lana ʿabidun): i.e., submissive and humbled, worshipping Us with praise and humility. "So that they may be guided" (laʿallahum yahtadun): the pronoun refers to the Children of Israel, not to the people of Pharaoh, because the latter perished before the Torah was revealed.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 50:

﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾ Al-rabwa (rabwah): the elevated place of the earth. It may be pronounced with the ra' vowelled with fatha, damma, or kasra. The scholars differed concerning the location of this rabwa. It was said: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was said: the Ghuta of Damascus. It was said: Palestine. ﴿with level ground and a flowing spring﴾ Al-qarar: the level part of the earth; its meaning is that it is a flat expanse in which tilling and planting are possible. It was also said that qarar here means fruits and grains. Al-ma'in is flowing water. It was said that it derives from your saying "ma'una al-ma'u" (the water became abundant), so the mim in this case is original, and its pattern is fa'il. It was said that it derives from al-'ayn (the spring), so the mim is augmentative, and its pattern is maf'ul.

﴿O messengers﴾. This address is not to be taken literally, because the messengers came at different times. The meaning is that each messenger, in his own time, was addressed with this. It has also been said that the address is to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and that he was put in the place of the group. This view is weak.

﴿Eat of the good things﴾. That is, of the lawful. On this reading the command is for obligation (wujub), or, if "good things" means the pleasant ones, the command is for permissibility (ibahah).

And indeed, ﴿this your community is one community﴾. It was read with a kasra on *inna*, as a resumed sentence (*istinaf*, a new clause), and this is the reading of the people of Kufa. It was also read with a fatha, meaning "because" (*li-anna*), and in that case it is connected to his words at the end, ﴿so fear Me﴾. It was said that it is connected to a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "and know." Here "community" (*ummah*) means the religion, which is what the messengers agreed upon, namely monotheism (*tawhid*) and other matters.

﴿So they divided their affair﴾, meaning they separated and disagreed. The pronoun refers to the nations of the messengers mentioned, including the Jews, the Christians, and others.

﴿Zuburan﴾ (زُبُراً) is the plural of زبور (zabur), which means a book. The meaning is that they split over following the scriptures. One group followed the Tawrah (Torah), another followed the Injil (Gospel), and others followed other books. They also produced a book of their own invention.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 54:

﴿So leave them in their bewilderment for a time﴾. The pronoun refers to the Quraysh. Al-ghamra (bewilderment) is ignorance and misguidance, and its origin is from ghamrat al-ma' (the surging of water, i.e. being submerged in water). ﴿For a time﴾ here means until the day of Badr, or until the day of their death.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verses 55–56:

﴿Do they think﴾ the verse: It refutes them regarding their assumption that their wealth and children are good for them, and that these are a cause of Allah's good pleasure with them. ﴿We hasten for them﴾ This is the predicate (khabar) of "anna" (the emphatic particle "that"), and the connecting pronoun is omitted, its implied form being "nusari'u bihi" (We hasten them with it). ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾ That is, they do not perceive that this is a gradual leading toward ruin (istidraj), so there is in it a sense of warning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 60:

﴿They give what they give﴾. It was said: its meaning is that they give what they have given of zakat (obligatory almsgiving) and charities. It was also said: it is general to all acts of righteousness, meaning they perform them while fearing that they will not be accepted from them. ʿĀʾisha narrated this meaning from the Prophet (ﷺ).

However, she recited: ﴿yu'tūna mā ātaw﴾ with the short vowel (qaṣr), so the hadith may be an explanation of this recitation. It was also said: it is general to good deeds and bad deeds, meaning they perform them while fearing a return to God ﴿that they will return to their Lord﴾. Anna (that) is in the position of the object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), or in the position of the object of wajila (to fear), since it carries the meaning of "fearful."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 61:

﴿Those are the ones who hasten toward the good things﴾. In this there are two meanings: first, that they hasten to perform acts of obedience; and second, that they seek to attain the reward of good deeds early. This matches the preceding verse, because it affirms for them the hastening that was denied to the disbelievers.

﴿And they are foremost in them﴾. In this there are the two meanings mentioned for "yusari'una lil-khayrat" (they hasten toward the good things). It has also been said that its meaning is: happiness was decreed for them in pre-eternity (al-azal).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 62:

﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity.﴾ He means that what the righteous were described as doing lies within their capacity and strength and is not beyond it. The discussion of imposing what cannot be borne has already been covered in Surat al-Baqarah. ﴿And with Us is a Book﴾ means the records of deeds (ṣaḥā'if al-a'mal). So the statement contains both a warning and an assurance against injustice and wrongdoing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verses 63–66:

﴿In a state of heedlessness concerning this﴾: that is, in heedlessness of the religion as a whole and of the Qur'an. It is also said: of the Book mentioned; and it is said: of the deeds with which the believers were described. ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾: that is, they have evil deeds beyond the heedlessness in which they are. The meaning, then, is that they combine disbelief with evil conduct. The reference of "that" (dhalika), on this view, is to the heedlessness (ghamra), and he referred to it with the emphatic form because it carries the meaning of disbelief. It is also said that the reference is to his words "concerning this" (min hadha): that is, they have evil deeds other than those already referred to, as has been disputed. ﴿They are doing them﴾: it is said that this is a report about their present deeds, and it is said that it concerns the future. It is also said that the meaning is that they persist in doing them until God seizes them, so He says ﴿until when We seize their affluent ones﴾. The phrase ﴿until when﴾ is the end point (ghayah) of his words ﴿doing﴾. ﴿Their affluent ones (mutrafin)﴾: that is, their wealthy and their chieftains. ﴿Behold, they cry out for help (yajarun)﴾: that is, they implore and shout. If by the punishment is meant the killing of the affluent ones on the day of Badr, then the pronoun in "yajarun" refers to the rest of Quraysh: that is, they shouted and wailed over the slain. If by the punishment is meant the hardships of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter, then the pronoun refers to all of them. ﴿Do not cry out for help today﴾: its implied sense is that it will be said to them on the day of punishment: "Do not cry out for help." It may be that this statement is literal, or that it is spoken through the tongue of the state, and its wording is a prohibition while its meaning is that crying out will not benefit them. ﴿Turning back on your heels, you retreat﴾: that is, you return backward, and this is an expression for their turning away from the signs, which are the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 67:

﴿Mustakbirīna bihi﴾ (arrogant regarding it). It has been said: the pronoun refers to the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). It has also been said: it refers to the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), even though it is not mentioned; rather, it is understood from the context of the speech. The meaning is that they act arrogantly because of the Sacred Mosque, since they are its people and its custodians. It has also been said: it refers to the Qur'an, from the standpoint that the verses were recited; the meaning on this view is that the Qur'an produces in them defiance and arrogance. It has also been said: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and on this view it is connected to ﴿sāmiran﴾ (conversing at night).

﴿Sāmiran﴾ is derived from al-samar, which is sitting at night for conversation. The Quraysh used to gather at night in the mosque and converse, and most of their talk was abusing the Prophet ﷺ. Sāmiran is singular in form but has the meaning of plural, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Whoever takes the pronoun in bihi to refer to the Prophet ﷺ, the meaning is that they converse at night mentioning him and reviling him.

﴿Tahjurūn﴾: whoever reads it with a dammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the jīm, its meaning is "you say al-hujr" with a dammah on the hā', which is obscene speech; this is the reading of Nafi'. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the jīm, so it derives from al-hajr with a fatḥah on the hā', meaning you abandon (tahjurūn) Islam, the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Or it derives from your saying "hajara al-marīḍ" when the sick person raves, meaning: you utter idle talk (al-laghw min al-qawl).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 68:

﴿Have they not then pondered over the Word?﴾ He means the Qur'an, and this is a rebuke to them. ﴿Or has there come to them that which did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ Its meaning is that prophethood is no novelty that they should deny it; rather, prophethood came to their forefathers of old, for prophethood was given to Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), and others.

Verse 23:69: ﴿Or did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ The meaning: Did they not recognize Muhammad (ﷺ), and know that he was the most noble of them, the most truthful in speech, the greatest in trustworthiness, and the most sound in intellect? How, then, do they attribute to him lying or madness, or any other deficiency? Yet he came to them with the truth, which is not hidden from anyone of sound intellect, and which is pure correctness.

Here "following" (ittiba') is a metaphor (isti'arah), and "the truth" (al-haqq) is meant to be right judgement and the straight course. The meaning is: if the matter were as their desires demand, namely associating partners with Allah and following falsehood, then the heavens and the earth would be corrupted, as in His saying: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. It has been said that the truth in the verse is Allah the Exalted, but this is far from the meaning. What led to it is that they took "following" literally and did not perceive the metaphor in it. The truth here is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Rather, he brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70]. As for His saying: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, it may mean that it is a reminder and admonition to them, or that it is their honour and nobility. This latter is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 72:

﴿Or do you ask them for any payment (kharj)?﴾ Al-kharj is the wage (al-ujra), and it is also said: kharaj (kharaj), and the meaning is one. It has been recited in both forms in the two places, so it is like His saying: ﴿Or do you ask them?﴾, i.e., you are not asking them for a wage, so that following you would be burdensome for them. ﴿But the payment (kharaj) of your Lord is better﴾, i.e., the provision of your Lord is better than their wealth; He provides for you and makes you independent of them.

Translation:

﴿Are indeed deviating from the path﴾ — that is, they are swerving away and turning aside from the straight path.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 23, verses 75–77**

﴿وَلَوْ رَحِمْنَاهُمْ﴾ [the verse] (*al-ayah*, "verse"): Most scholars said: This verse was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against Quraysh that they be struck by drought, so hunger befell them until they ate hides and other things. The meaning is: "Even if We had shown them mercy by granting them abundance and removed the harm of hunger and drought that afflicts them, they would persist in their transgression." In my view, however, there is a problem with this, because the verse is Meccan by unanimous agreement, and the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against Quraysh only after the Hijrah (migration to Medina), as stated in the hadith (prophetic tradition). It has also been said: The meaning is, "Even if We had mercy upon them by returning them to the world, they would return to what they had been forbidden." This view does not entail what the previous one entails, but it departs from the meaning of the verse.

﴿وَلَقَدْ أَخَذْنَاهُمْ بِٱلْعَذَابِ﴾ It has been said: This punishment is hunger caused by drought, and the gate of severe punishment that they were threatened with after this is the Day of Badr. This is rejected, because the punishment that befell them was after Badr. It has also been said: The punishment that seized them was the Day of Badr, and the gate they were threatened with is drought. It has further been said: "The gate of severe punishment" is the punishment of the Hereafter, and this is the stronger view. Therefore He described it as severe, because it is more severe than the punishment of this world. And He said:

﴿إِذَا هُمْ فِيهِ مُبْلِسُونَ﴾ [then they will be in despair therein], meaning: they will be in despair of good. Their despair will occur in the Hereafter, as in His saying: ﴿وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ ٱلسَّاعَةُ يُبْلِسُ ٱلْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ [And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will be in despair] [al-Rum: 12].

﴿فَمَا ٱسْتَكَانُواْ﴾ [Yet they did not humble themselves], meaning: they did not humble themselves before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The discussion of this word has already preceded at the end of Al ʿImran [146].

﴿وَمَا يَتَضَرَّعُونَ﴾ [nor did they supplicate humbly]. If it is asked: Why did He not say "فما استكانوا وما تضرعوا" (fa-ma istakanu wa-ma tadarra'u), or "فما يستكينون وما يتضرعون" (fa-ma yastakinuna wa-ma yatadarra'una), so that both verbs agree in tense, either past or future? The answer: "ما استكانوا" refers to their humbling at the punishment that struck them, while "وما يتضرعون" refers to their not supplicating until a gate of severe punishment is opened upon them. Thus He negated humbling in the past, and negated supplication in the present and future.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 84–90:

﴿Say, "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?"﴾ These verses are a questioning of them about matters they cannot deny, and if they acknowledge them, it necessarily follows that they must affirm the oneness of their Creator and believe in the Hereafter. ﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ The first (lillah, "to Allah") is read with the lam (la) by consensus, as a reply to His saying: ﴿To whom belongs the earth﴾. Likewise the majority read the second and third, and this is according to the meaning, because His saying ﴿Who is the Lord of the seven heavens﴾ carries the sense of "to whom belongs". Abu 'Amr read the second and third with the raf' (lafza, "Allah" in the nominative, i.e., according to the wording) according to the wording. Malakut is a verbal noun (masdar), and its pattern (binā') carries intensification (mubalagha) of meaning. ﴿He protects, and none can protect against Him﴾. Al-ijara (protection) means preventing harm or humiliation. It is said: "I gave protection (ajart) to so-and-so against so-and-so" when you prevent him from harm and humiliation by that person. So the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, grants relief to whomever He wills from whomever He wills, and none can grant relief from Him to anyone. ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ That is, you are deceived away from the truth, and the one who deceives them is Satan. This is a likening to magic in confusion and falling into falsehood. He arranged these three rebukes in gradation: He first said: ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ Then He said second: ﴿Will you not fear Allah?﴾ and this is more eloquent, because it contains added warning. Then He said third: ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ and in it is a rebuke not found in the others. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, meaning in what they attribute to Allah of partners and offspring, and for this reason He refuted them by negating that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 23, verse 91:

﴿Since (in that case) every god would have taken away what he created﴾ This is a proof of God's oneness (tawhid al-uluhiyya, the unity of divinity). Its explanation is that it is said: If there were with God another god, each one of them would have been alone with his creation apart from the creation of the other, and each one of them would have been arrogant with his dominion, and each would have sought to overcome the other and to be exalted over him, as you see the condition of the kings of this world. But since we see all created things linked to one another, so that the whole world is as if it were a single sphere, we know that its owner and its governor is one, and there is no god besides Him. This proof is not the argument of mutual prevention (dalil al-tamana', the argument from mutual obstruction) as Ibn 'Atiyya and others understood it; rather it is a different proof. If it is said: "idhan" (then, in that case) is only entered upon a statement that is a condition and a response; how, then, did it enter here when no condition had preceded it and no questioner had asked? The answer: the condition is elided, its implied sense being "if there were with Him gods," and it was elided because of the indication of His words: ﴿and there was not with Him any god﴾. It is a response to the disbelievers against whom the refutation was directed.

﴿from the whisperings of the devils﴾ meaning their prompting and their insinuations. It is also said: it means madness, though the wording is more general than that. ﴿and that they should be present with me﴾ means that they should be with him. It is also said: it means their presence at the time of death. ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾ Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Here ḥattā (until) is a particle of beginning, meaning that it is not an end-point of what precedes it." al-Zamakhshari said: "ḥattā is connected to yaṣifūn (they describe), meaning: they will not cease to be so until death comes to them." ﴿He says: "My Lord, send me back,"﴾ meaning a return to the world. He addressed this in the plural form as a mark of honour, as al-Zamakhshari and others said, and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"Ah, then have mercy on me, O family of Muhammad."

It is also said that he called upon his Lord and then addressed the angels. ﴿so that I may act righteously in what I have left behind.﴾ It is said: it means what he has left behind of wealth. It is also said: it means what he has left behind of faith. This is like His saying: ﴿or [who] earned good through his faith [before]﴾ [al-Anʿam: 158]. The meaning is that the disbeliever desires to return to the world so that he may believe and do righteous deeds in the faith that he abandoned the first time. ﴿No! It is merely a word he is saying.﴾ A rebuke to him concerning what he asked for. ﴿It is merely a word he is saying﴾ means his statement: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ ﴿so that I may act righteously.﴾ He called this speech a "word" (kalimah), and regarding the interpretation of its meaning there are three opinions: first, that he will certainly say this word because of the excess of his regret and anguish, so it is a report of his own utterance. Second, that the meaning is that it is a word he says which neither benefits him nor avails him anything. Third, that the meaning is that he says it falsely, and that even if he were returned to the world he would not act righteously. ﴿And behind them﴾ means in what they will face of time to come, and the pronoun refers to the group mentioned in His saying "when death comes to one of them." ﴿is a barzakh﴾ means the period between death and the Resurrection, and it stands as a barrier between them and their return to the world. The original meaning of barzakh is a barrier between two things. ﴿So there will be no kinship between them﴾ The meaning is that on that Day the mutual compassion and tenderness that exist among relatives will cease, because each person is occupied with himself, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father﴾ [ʿAbasa: 34–35], so kinship will be as though it did not exist. ﴿Nor will they ask one another.﴾ That is, no one will ask another, because each is occupied with himself. If it is asked: how can this be reconciled with His saying: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning one another﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 25]? The answer is that the abandoning of questioning occurs at the first blast of the Trumpet, and afterwards they will question one another, for the Day of Resurrection is a long day in which there are many standing places.

The Fire will scorch their faces, ﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾, meaning it will touch them with burning, ﴿grim-faced﴾. Kulooh (grimacing, baring the teeth) is the drawing back of the lips from the teeth. This often happens to dogs, and it may also happen to rams when their heads are roasted. In a hadith: "The lip of the disbeliever will be drawn up in the Fire until it reaches the middle of his head," and in that there is punishment and disfigurement.
﴿Our wretchedness overcame us﴾: i.e., the wretchedness that was decreed for them. It is also read as شقاوتنا, and the meaning is the same.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 23, verse 108:

﴿He will say, "Be silent and do not speak to Me."﴾ The word (ukhsa'u, "be silent/begone") is used to drive away dogs, so it contains humiliation and banishment. ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ means: do not speak to Me about lifting the punishment. At that, they despair of that. May Allah protect us from that by His mercy.

﴿سِخْرِيّاً﴾ [sikhriyyan] with a ḍamma on the sīn, from al-sukhrah (servitude, being made to serve), and with a kasra, from al-sikhr (mockery). It may also be said with a ḍamma. It is read here in both ways because both meanings are possible. The meaning of mockery is more fitting here, given His words ﴿and you used to laugh at them﴾.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 23, verses 112–115:

﴿How many years did you remain on the earth?﴾ That is, in the depths of the earth as dead people. It is also said: alive in the world. They answered that they had stayed a day or part of a day, either because they considered the duration short, or because of the torment they were in, such that they counted nothing else. ﴿So ask those who count﴾ That is, ask those who are able to count. It is said they mean those who were spared from what they had been tried with, or that they mean the angels. ﴿If you had remained only a little﴾ Its meaning: in comparison with your remaining in Hell, abiding forever. ﴿In vain﴾ That is, in falsehood. The meaning is the establishment of proof for the Resurrection, for reward and punishment.

Qur'anic quotations: "There is no proof for him of it" — meaning: no argument and no evidence. The clause is a description of His words "another god" (ilahan akhar). The answer to the condition is "Then his reckoning is only with his Lord; indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed." The pronoun (in "innahu") refers to the matter and the situation (al-amr wa'l-sha'n). Consider how He opened the surah with the success of the believers and closed it with the non-success of the disbelievers, to show the gap between the two groups, and God knows best.
